title: Sort the People
description: Sort names by their corresponding heights descending, using an index array to keep parallel arrays synchronized through the sort.

blocks.text: Given names[] and heights[] (heights are distinct, names may repeat), where names[i] corresponds to heights[i], return names sorted in descending order by height.

blocks.caption: Sorting by index keeps each name paired with its own height throughout the sort.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","names[] and heights[] (parallel arrays, heights distinct)"],["Output","names[] reordered so heights would be strictly descending"]]}

blocks.text: Sorting one array based on the values of a PARALLEL array is a classic index-sorting pattern: rather than sorting the names directly (which would lose the name-height correspondence), sort the INDICES using the height array as the comparison key, then read out the names in that index order.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: Sorting indices instead of values directly is the standard way to keep multiple parallel arrays synchronized through a sort.

Picture a team roster where each name has a height tag attached. To line everyone up tallest to shortest, sort by the height tags, keeping each name attached to its own tag throughout, then read off just the names in the new order.

blocks.caption: Each name stays attached to its own height throughout the sort.

items: Sort those indices using heights[index] as the descending comparison key.
Build the result by reading names[index] for each sorted index.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Sorted by height descending: 180 (Mary), 170 (Emma), 165 (John), giving ["Mary", "Emma", "John"], matching the expected output exactly.
A direct approach could bubble-sort the (name, height) pairs together as combined units, swapping both arrays in lockstep whenever a swap is needed. This is correct but quadratic.

Sorting an index array with a comparator that looks up heights[index] achieves the same synchronized reordering using an efficient built-in sort, without needing to physically move both arrays in tandem during every comparison step.
Bubble-sort both arrays together, swapping the corresponding name and height whenever a height is out of the desired descending order.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n^2)","Bubble sort compares and swaps repeatedly"],["Space","O(n)","The cloned name and height arrays"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: A quadratic sort is unnecessary once an efficient built-in sort can be applied to an index array instead.
Build an index array [0, 1, ..., n-1] and sort it using a comparator based on heights[index], descending. Build the final result by mapping each sorted index back to its name.

items: Sort those indices by heights[index] descending, O(n log n).
Map each sorted index to names[index] to build the result.

codes.python:
def sort_people(names, heights):
    n = len(names)
    indices = list(range(n))
    indices.sort(key=lambda i: -heights[i])
    return [names[i] for i in indices]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(sort_people(["Mary", "John", "Emma"], [180, 165, 170]))
    print(sort_people(["Alice", "Bob", "Bob"], [155, 185, 150]))

items: Sorting one array based on values from a parallel array is best done by sorting an INDEX array, not the values directly.
This keeps every parallel array correctly synchronized through the sort, since the index uniquely identifies each element across all arrays.
This index-sort pattern generalizes to sorting by ANY number of parallel arrays or derived keys at once.

blocks.text: Sort the People is solved by sorting an index array using the heights array as the comparison key (descending), then reading out the names in that sorted index order. This keeps names and heights correctly paired throughout an efficient O(n log n) sort.
